lessons.title: How a diesel engine works
lessons.html:
The four-stroke diesel engine

Almost all tractors use a four-stroke diesel engine. Inside each cylinder a piston moves up and down. The piston is joined to the crankshaft by a connecting rod. The crankshaft turns the up-and-down movement into turning movement that drives the tractor.

The four strokes

  1. Intake: the piston moves down and the intake valve opens. Air is sucked or pushed into the cylinder. A diesel takes in air only, not fuel.
  2. Compression: both valves close and the piston moves up, squeezing the air. Squeezed air gets very hot.
  3. Power: near the top, the injector sprays diesel into the hot air. The fuel burns by itself, without a spark plug. The hot gas pushes the piston down.
  4. Exhaust: the exhaust valve opens and the piston moves up, pushing the burnt gas out.

The camshaft opens and closes the valves at the right time. It is driven by gears or a belt from the crankshaft.

Main engine parts

  • Cylinder block: the main body with the cylinders.
  • Cylinder head: on top, holds valves and injectors.
  • Head gasket: seals between head and block.
  • Pistons and rings: rings seal the piston in the cylinder.
  • Crankshaft, connecting rods and bearings.
  • Flywheel: heavy wheel that smooths the engine and carries the clutch.
  • Sump: holds the engine oil at the bottom.

Turbocharger

Many tractors have a turbocharger. Exhaust gas spins a turbine that drives a compressor, pushing more air into the engine. More air means more fuel can be burnt and more power made. Let a turbo engine idle for a short while before switching off so the turbo can cool and keep its oil supply.

lessons.title: Fuel, air, cooling and lubrication systems
lessons.html:
The systems that keep the engine alive

Air system

The engine needs clean air. On a dusty farm the air filter does a big job. Dust that gets past the filter wears the cylinders like sandpaper. Check the filter indicator, clean or replace the element as the manual says, and check that hoses and clamps have no leaks.

Fuel system

Diesel goes from the tank, through a water separator and filters, to the injection pump and injectors. Diesel must be clean. Water and dirt damage injection parts, which are very costly. Drain water from the separator, change filters on time, and keep fuel drums and bowsers clean and closed. If air gets into the system, the engine will not run until it is bled as the manual shows.

Cooling system

Burning fuel makes a lot of heat. The cooling system carries heat away using coolant pumped through the engine to the radiator. Parts include the water pump, thermostat, radiator, fan, hoses and pressure cap. Keep the radiator fins clean of grass seeds and chaff. Use the coolant type the manual says. Never open the cap when hot.

Lubrication system

Oil is pumped from the sump through a filter to bearings, the camshaft, pistons and turbo. Oil reduces wear, cools parts and carries dirt to the filter. Check the dipstick daily with the tractor level and the engine stopped. Use the oil grade in the manual and change oil and filter at the stated hours.

Warning signs

SignPossible problem
Oil pressure light onLow oil or pump problem: stop the engine at once
Temperature gauge highLow coolant, blocked radiator, broken fan belt
Black smokeBlocked air filter, overload, injector fault
White smokeCold engine, water in fuel or coolant leak
Blue smokeEngine burning oil

Key points

  • A diesel has intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes and no spark plug.
  • Dust in the air system wears the engine quickly.
  • Clean fuel and timely filter changes protect the injection system.
  • Keep radiators clean and never open a hot cap.
  • Stop the engine at once if the oil pressure light comes on.

quiz.question: How does diesel fuel ignite in the cylinder?

options.text: By the heat of compressed air

quiz.question: In which stroke does the hot gas push the piston down?

options.text: Pushes more air into the engine
